title: FDA approves pioneering breast cancer drug that nips resistance in the bud - Nature Biotechnology
text:
Download PDF

A breast cancer drug linked with a test to detect ESR1 mutations in circulating tumor DNA is one of a wave of new drugs developed to tackle resistance to estrogen-receptor-targeted therapies.

On 4 September the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved AstraZeneca’s pill Etcamah (camizestrant) for a subset of patients with estrogen receptor (ER)-positive breast cancer who acquire resistance mutations during treatment. This approval is the first based on a circulating tumor DNA blood test designed to detect when mutations in the estrogen receptor gene ESR1 have emerged. The test identifies these genetic changes early, allowing doctors to switch breast cancer treatments before disease progression shows up on a standard scan.Mutations in the estrogen receptor lead to resistance to hormone therapies in breast cancer.
Credit: Science Picture Co/Alamy“It’s a great idea,” says Angela DeMichele, an oncologist specializing in breast cancer at the Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania. “We switch the person’s therapy away from the drug that they are now theoretically resistant to, to a different drug that they should now be sensitive to,” she says.Suzanne Wardell, a cancer pharmacologist at Duke University School of Medicine, agrees that this approach might improve patient outcomes “because you’re nipping those mutant cells in the bud, before they can really cause further metastasis and greater disease,” she says.ER-positive breast cancers are the most common subtype of the disease, encompassing ~70% of patients, and they respond well to targeted hormone therapies. First-line treatments such as selective ER modulators that inhibit ER signaling and aromatase inhibitors that block estrogen production have been used for more than 30 years. In the last decade, combining endocrine blockers with cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 (CDK4/6) has substantially improved outcomes for advanced or metastatic ER-positive, HER2-negative tumors.But, in about 40% of patients receiving endocrine treatment and a CDK4/6 inhibitor, cancers become resistant. The emerging mutations in ESR1 keep ER switched on in tumors so cancers keep on growing even in the absence of estrogen.The preferred treatment option for patients who have stopped responding to first-line therapies is Faslodex (fulvestrant), which was approved in 2002 and is also itself used as a first-line therapy. Fulvestrant is an ER antagonist and selective ER degrader (SERD), but it is far from an ideal drug. “It’s intramuscular, it’s clunky, it doesn’t have the best pharmacokinetics, and it has really poor activity post-CDK4/6,” says Erika Hamilton, an oncologist and director of breast cancer research at Sarah Cannon Research Institute in Nashville.AstraZeneca’s Etcamah is a next-generation oral SERD and complete ER antagonist. It is one of a growing group of next-generation oral drugs (Table 1) identified in the long-running search to improve on fulvestrant. All these drugs share the goal of retaining anti-estrogen activity in ESR1-mutant cancers, but the program for Etcamah also tested a new hypothesis: that switching to the drug as soon as ESR1 mutations are detected using circulating tumor DNA, as opposed to remaining on first-line therapy until tumors became evident on radiographic images, can be advantageous to patients.Table 1 Selected ER antagonists or inhibitors approved or in clinical trials for ER-positive breast cancerFull size tableThe aim is to maintain the anti-estrogen and CDK4/6 inhibitor pairing activity, since CDK4/6 inhibitors do not work well on their own. “If you can tweak the endocrine therapy, you can continue the excellent CDK4/6 inhibitor combination, which we know is very good for patients,” says Teresa Klinowska, global product leader for oncology at AstraZeneca. “Our hypothesis was to prolong that period for as long as possible.”The hypothesis has now been confirmed. The FDA and European Medicines Agency approvals of Etcamah are based on the results of a trial known as SERENA-6, which involved more than 3,000 patients receiving first-line treatment with an aromatase inhibitor plus a CDK4/6 inhibitor for ER-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer. Switching the aromatase inhibitor to Etcamah at ESR1 mutation emergence increased progression-free survival by more than 7 months, to 16.8 months, compared to continuing treatment with the aromatase inhibitor. The switch to Etcamah also increased second progression-free survival — the time to progression after a next-line therapy — by over 6 months. This finding “gives confidence to physicians and patients that the benefit is long-lasting,” says Klinowska.Other oral SERDs that have also superseded fulvestrant include Veppanu (vepdegestrant), developed by Arvinas and Pfizer and approved in May 2026. Veppanu works by a pioneering PROTAC (proteolysis-targeting chimera) degrader mechanism.Veppanu is a heterobifunctional degrader that works by binding with one arm to the ER and with another to the E3 ligase in the ubiquitin–proteasome system, the cell’s protein recycling system. In its pivotal trial, treatment with Veppanu delayed disease progression or death by about 3 months compared with standard-of-care in a subgroup of about 270 patients with ESR1 mutations who had received up to three previous therapies.Its developers had hoped that Veppanu’s novel pharmacology would result in improved outcomes regardless of ESR1 mutation status. However, in patients without ESR1 mutations, Veppanu did not improve outcomes. Disease in people without ESR1 mutations was “driven through other mechanisms,” says Angela Cacace, Arvinas’s CSO.The narrower approvable indication was one factor in Pfizer’s decision to downscale their development plans for Veppanu in 2025, with Rigel licensing the rights to commercialize the drug from Arvinas and Pfizer in May 2026.Other drug developers have also had mixed success in their attempts to develop new oral ER-targeted therapies that improve outcomes in wider populations receiving therapy for ER-positive breast cancer, rather than just patients with ESR1 mutations. “We’ve seen time and time again in clinical trials that patients with estrogen-receptor activating mutations are the ones that get great clinical benefit,” says Wardell.For example, Menarini’s drug Orserdu (elacestrant) was tested in patients with ER-positive, HER2-negative advanced or metastatic breast cancer with disease progression following at least one line of endocrine therapy in a phase 3 trial known as EMERALD. However, the benefit observed was largely driven by patients with ESR1 mutations, and the drug’s FDA approval in 2023 was restricted to this group.Eli Lilly’s Inluriyo (imlunestrant) similarly failed to significantly increase progression-free survival in the full ER-positive, HER2-negative population in a phase 3 trial known as EMBER-3 but also showed benefit in patients with ESR1 mutations. It received FDA approval for this patient subgroup in September 2025.Ideally, however, treatment with the latest generation of ER-targeted therapies should not have to wait for arising ESR1 mutations to be implemented. “I think we’re going to be hearing more about these compounds in earlier lines because they’re just as well tolerated, if not better, than aromatase inhibitors,” says Hamilton. “And they certainly are showing good activity,” she says. Hamilton was involved in the trials of ER blockers from Arvinas, Olema Oncology, AstraZeneca and Eli Lilly.AstraZeneca’s next readout for Etcamah, expected later this year, is from the SERENA-4 trial, which is testing the compound in patients who have not previously received drug therapy for advanced disease. The company is also testing Etcamah versus endocrine therapy in patients with early breast cancer in the CAMBRIA-1 and CAMBRIA-2 trials that are expected to read out next year. “We hope with our CAMBRIA trials that we’ll actually be able to cure patients to stop their disease recurring at all,” says AstraZeneca’s Klinowska.Another drug being tested as a first-line treatment is Olema Oncology’s palazestrant, which is in phase 3 trials in advanced breast cancer in combination with a CDK4/6 inhibitor. Palazestrant and several other next-generation ER blockers have a dual mechanism; they inhibit ERs directly — a so-called complete ER antagonist (CERAN) — and also have a SERD mechanism that activates the ubiquitin–proteasome pathway, leading to ER destabilization and degradation. Developers now think the SERD action is secondary to antagonism. “It was always our intention to go after a complete estrogen receptor antagonist,” says Olema CEO Sean Bohen, believing this mechanism could better control growth and proliferation in ER-positive cancer cells than drugs that work primarily as degraders. “You need to shut the signal off completely,” he says.Olema’s palazestrant and other ER blockers in this class, such as Etcamah and Genentech/Roche’s giredestrant, work, at least in part, by blocking both of the ER regions that control transcriptional activity: the AF2 estrogen-binding domain and the ligand-independent AF1 domain. “If the ER is bound by these [drug] molecules, it’s locked in an inactive conformation,” says Bohen. Olema’s poster at the 2026 American Association for Cancer Research (AACR) meeting shows that palazestrant binds to AF2 directly and blocks AF1 by recruiting a nuclear co-repressor protein to this site. Blocking AF1 could prevent oncogenic kinases from cross-talking with ERs and activating estrogen-independent transcription.Roche/Genentech’s IidERA trial of giredestrant in early breast cancer stands out as “it’s one of the first [to show efficacy] that’s not limited to the ESR1 population,” says Hamilton, who was not involved in the trial. LidERA showed that patients who received giredestrant after tumor surgery were 30% less likely to develop invasive disease progression than people who received standard-of-care, such as an aromatase inhibitor. On the basis of these data, the FDA is set to make an approval decision by 30 November 2026.When Genentech researchers investigated giredestrant’s mechanism, they found it and other drugs in this class work, at least in part, by stopping the ER from moving around within the nucleus. “We think that immobilization is the source of the potency of these molecules,” says Ciara Metcalfe, director of discovery oncology at Genentech. When ER movement is restricted, transcription is halted. Genentech’s published work shows that this mechanism precedes ER degradation, although researchers are not sure yet how immobilization occurs.Nevertheless, giredestrant missed the primary progression-free survival endpoint in a separate trial, persevERA, which tested the drug in patients who had not previously had treatment for metastatic disease. But Metcalfe is optimistic. “I see persevERA as being the first shot on goal [for front-line metastatic disease], but certainly not the end of the story,” she says. Genentech intends to use circulating tumor DNA samples taken throughout the trial to better understand how giredestrant shapes ER-driven tumors in metastatic disease and the types of mutations that drive disease — new kinds of ER mutations or ER bypass mutations, for example — as tumor burden increases. This information could aid the design of ER-antagonist trials “that deal with tumor evolution on the fly — studies that will let us respond to the tumor biology,” says Metcalfe. “We are on the cusp of seeing that data.”Clinicians, too, need better ways to determine which patients will respond to ER inhibitors. “That’s what is going to be the next real challenge,” says Wardell, who holds intellectual property related to Menarini’s Orserdu. Assays that measure ER activity, not just its expression or mutation status, are coming online. Precede Biosciences’ so-called PERDI assay, for instance, measures the transcriptional activity of ERs in blood samples via histone modifications and DNA methylation. It identified patients most likely to benefit from giredestrant, including those without ESR1-mutated disease, according to data presented at AACR 2026.Estrogen receptors have long taken center stage as a breast cancer target, beginning with the discovery of the SERM tamoxifen 60 years ago, and will continue to do so. “We’ve not found another node in the progression of breast cancer that is so critical, says DeMichele. “A node that once shut down provides long-term disease control or elimination, with low toxicity.”
